articles.title: Thailand welcomes US-Myanmar engagement, expects ASEAN talks on country's future - Yahoo News Singapore
articles.summary: Thailand welcomes US-Myanmar engagement, expects ASEAN talks on country's future  Yahoo News Singapore
articles.full_text:
By Sergio Goncalves and Miguel Pereira
LISBON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Thailand welcomes US engagement with Myanmar and expects discussions at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations' November summit in Manila on how to proceed with the member barred since the 2021 coup, Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told Reuters on Friday.
The United States and Myanmar's military-backed government held talks in Tokyo two weeks ago, their second meeting in a month as Washington steps up re-engagement with the generals it shunned after the coup.
"We don't want to see Myanmar isolated, we don't want Myanmar to be an arena for geopolitical rivalry ... so the US engagement is something that we welcome," he said.
Engagement "does not mean legitimizing the regime," but aims to encourage peaceful conflict resolution and reconciliation with the opposition, Sihasak, who is also deputy prime minister, added.
He said there was "some shift in ASEAN's position," citing Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing's recent visits to Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand and Malaysia, but said it was unclear whether the Manila summit would address restoring Myanmar's full representation.
"It's good that we're going to have a very substantive, very extensive, and very in-depth discussion on how to proceed on Myanmar," he said.
He also said Thailand and Cambodia could resolve their longstanding land and maritime boundary disputes within 12 to 18 months despite limited progress.
"It is possible, everything is possible," he said, cautioning that confidence-building and addressing security concerns along the land border, where clashes have occurred, must come first.
Cambodia launched a conciliation process under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea in June to resolve the maritime boundary dispute, after Thailand terminated a 2001 joint development framework in May following deadly border clashes. The first meeting was held about a month ago.
"Right now, we haven't achieved, to be very frank, much progress," he said.
The maritime dispute centers on overlapping claims to about 26,000 sq km in the Gulf of Thailand, believed to hold oil and gas reserves worth around $300 billion. Thailand wants the boundary defined before discussing resource-sharing, he said.
Thailand-EU free-trade talks are in their final stage and could conclude by year-end if there is mutual political will, he added.
(Reporting by Sergio Goncalves and Miguel Pereira in Lisbon; Editing by Matthew Lewis)

articles.summary: Japanese FDI supports green transition in Vietnam’s manufacturing sector  Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.full_text:
Ho Chi Minh City (VNA) – Japanese Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is strengthening Vietnam’s manufacturing capacity and accelerating the green transition, as more Japanese companies expand production and adopt sustainable industrial solutions. 
Vietnam has become an important market and strategic manufacturing base in Southeast Asia for Japanese investors, reflecting their long-term confidence in the country’s economic potential and sustainable growth prospects. 
Investment cooperation has been a key pillar of Vietnam-Japan economic ties. According to the Vietnam Trade Promotion Agency under the Ministry of Industry and Trade, Japan has more than 5,800 active investment projects in Vietnam, with total registered capital exceeding 81 billion USD. 
Free trade agreements (FTAs) have also created favourable conditions for businesses in both countries through tariff reductions, rules of origin, and trade facilitation, opening up opportunities for deeper participation in regional production networks and supply chains. 
Major Japanese companies, including Honda, Panasonic, Kao Vietnam and Sumitomo, have maintained and expanded their operations in Vietnam. Meanwhile, new Japanese investment is flowing into industrial parks, supporting greener manufacturing and the adoption of more sustainable production solutions. 
A recent example is Japanese group Oji’s launch of construction of a new aseptic carton packaging factory under its Oji Liquid Pak (OLP) brand. The project, with an investment of 110 million USD, is located in Long Thanh High-Tech Park in Dong Nai province. 
The investment demonstrates Oji Liquid Pak’s long-term commitment to Vietnam and reinforces the country’s role as a strategic manufacturing and supply hub for the group in Southeast Asia. It is also expected to support the region’s shift towards circular packaging solutions that meet evolving policy requirements. 
Nguyen Quoc An, deputy head of the Dong Nai Industrial and Economic Zones Authority (DNIEZA), said large-scale projects like this would contribute to local industrial development, strengthen domestic production capacity and help Vietnamese businesses participate more deeply in regional supply chains. 
The authority pledged to support investors throughout project implementation, provide timely guidance and coordinate efforts to resolve difficulties so that projects can proceed in line with regulations and begin operations as soon as possible. 
Oji Liquid Pak General Director Kestutis Sliuzas said manufacturing industries, including packaging, were moving towards new standards that combine state-of-the-art recyclable materials and packaging, efficiency, and food safety. 
The new factory will combine food packaging production with research and development, technical services, and the installation and maintenance of Japanese machinery and equipment. These activities are expected to contribute to a modern industrial environment with higher quality and added value. 
Japanese investment also covers research and development in natural sciences, machinery repair and maintenance, equipment installation, and the import, export, and distribution of goods in accordance with Vietnamese law. 
Tran Viet Ha, Deputy Head of the Ho Chi Minh City Export Processing and Industrial Zones Authority (HEPZA), said the authority was working to help investors start projects sooner after registration and reduce procedures related to planning and construction. 
HEPZA aims to resolve matters within its authority directly and coordinate with other agencies on issues requiring inter-agency cooperation. It is also shifting from a focus on administrative procedures to monitoring projects throughout their life cycle, from investment preparation to operation. 
These efforts align with Politburo Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW, dated June 8, 2026, on developing the foreign-invested economy. The resolution shifts Vietnam’s investment attraction strategy towards quality rather than quantity, prioritising high technology, innovation, workforce development and technology transfer. 
The policy direction reflects Vietnam’s ambition to move beyond labour-intensive assembly towards becoming a technology-driven investment destination that generates higher added value and supports sustainable industrial growth./.

articles.full_text:
Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) and the Bank of Thailand (BOT) have joined the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s (MAS) BLOOM initiative as policymaker members.
The three central banks will work with industry players to develop common approaches for accepting, exchanging and settling digital money across borders.
Launched in October 2025, BLOOM (Borderless, Liquid, Open, Online, Multi-currency) brings together policymakers, financial institutions, payment networks and technology providers.
It supports settlement involving tokenised bank liabilities and regulated stablecoins.
Visa, Mastercard and Ripple among new participants
MAS also announced that Airwallex, Mastercard, Maybank, Monee, Nium, Ripple, ShopeePay, Visa and the World Bank Group have joined the initiative.
Participants are developing digital money applications across payments, treasury and trade finance.
The World Bank Group will contribute its experience in payment systems modernisation, cross-border payments and financial inclusion.
Three areas of cooperation
BLOOM will focus on three areas: cross-border acceptance and settlement, interoperability between digital money systems, and programmable controls. These controls include identity verification and sanctions screening.
MAS said common implementation frameworks would reduce the need for separate arrangements with counterparties or markets. This would lower implementation costs and shorten time to market.
Leong Sing Chiong, Deputy Managing Director (Markets and Development), MAS, said,
“To fully harness the benefits of using digital money, collaboration among policymakers and industry participants will be needed to address practical issues around acceptance, settlement and interoperability.”
Aznan bin Abdul Aziz, Deputy Governor, BNM, said,
“A future where frictionless cross-border payments can be made using multiple digital monies is now closer to a tangible reality than a far-fetched fantasy. BNM looks forward to exploring such a future through the BLOOM initiative with all participating central banks and industry partners.”
BLOOM builds on Project Orchid, an earlier MAS initiative that explored a digital Singapore dollar and its supporting infrastructure.

articles.title: Ripple BLOOM Initiative Expands As Malaysia And Thailand Join Singapore - TronWeekly
articles.summary: Ripple BLOOM Initiative Expands As Malaysia And Thailand Join Singapore  TronWeekly
articles.full_text:
The Ripple BLOOM Initiative has garnered some traction as Singapore extends its cross-border payment initiative with the inclusion of the central banks of Malaysia and Thailand from October 23, 2026.
Table of Contents
Headed by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), this initiative seeks to enhance international payments through the use of regulated stablecoins and tokenized bank deposits.
This development introduces more regional policymakers into the discourse surrounding digital currency standards and payment facilitation in Southeast Asia. Meanwhile, Cross River is incorporating Ripple’s RLUSD stablecoin based on the XRP ledger into its banking core system.
Also Read | Circle Shareholder Sues Trump Over $2B UAE Crypto Deals
What Is the Ripple BLOOM Initiative?
Ripple BLOOM Initiative is a growing topic of debate on Ripple’s stablecoin innovations and Singapore’s BLOOM project that addresses cross-border payment improvements. BLOOM stands for Borderless, Liquid, Open, Online, Multi-currency and is being spearheaded by MAS in partnership with the private sector.
MAS initiated the BLOOM project on October 16, 2025, in order to investigate how banks can leverage blockchain-enabled money in the process of international settlement. This project involves two types of digital money: tokenized bank liabilities and regulated stablecoins.
Tokenized bank liabilities are essentially tokenized bank deposits, whereas stablecoins are tokens whose aim is to hold stable value relative to some currency like the US dollar.
The Ripple BLOOM Initiative is related to general digital payment advancements, but the Singapore BLOOM project and Ripple RLUSD initiative are entirely different projects with separate objectives.
Malaysia and Thailand Join Singapore’s BLOOM Initiative
BNM and BOT became members of BLOOM among policymakers on October 23, 2026. This means that both central banks will have an opportunity to influence the development of the standards for digital currency and international transactions.
This project includes several organizations from the private sector, including Circle (stablecoin issuer), DBS (Singapore bank), Stripe (payments provider), and the World Bank Group.
The Ripple BLOOM Initiative is connected with the broader topic of digital payments because of the growing importance of stablecoins as instruments for interbank payments. However, Malaysia and Thailand became participants in Singapore’s BLOOM project.
BLOOM focuses mostly on wholesale finance activities and not retail payment transactions. This is done through trade finance and corporate treasury management, where companies require transfers of huge amounts of money across national borders.
Through the establishment of common standards, participating entities hope to cut down costs of payments, streamline the settlement process, and avoid country-specific arrangements.
How the Ripple BLOOM Initiative Relates to Stablecoin Payments
The Ripple BLOOM Initiative would serve as a good keyword for analyzing the trend towards blockchain-based payments despite BLOOM being an initiative by MAS. The goal of this project is to enhance cross-border payments by streamlining the transfer and settlement of digital currencies and deposits.
One of the main focus areas of the BLOOM Initiative is programmable compliance. It involves incorporating rules like sanctions screening and limits on transfers into the payment process.
BLOOM is also looking into ways to distribute the settlement assets, the possibility of having multiple currencies, and connecting various payment networks. The establishment of risk management standards is another one of BLOOM’s objectives.
In case these attempts prove successful, businesses will be able to transfer funds between the participating markets with ease. But this depends on how the standards are developed and implemented.
BLOOM by Ripple Initiative does not constitute a partnership or payment network by Ripple. Malaysia and Thailand will participate in shaping the standards for BLOOM, but cross-border stablecoin offerings have not yet been introduced.
BLOOM Builds on Singapore’s Project Orchid
The BLOOM project of Singapore extends the scope of the earlier Project Orchid initiated by MAS in 2021 for studying the digital version of the Singapore dollar.
The Ripple BLOOM Initiative discussion represents yet another attempt to bridge blockchain and traditional finance. The involvement of Malaysia and Thailand can lead to more collaboration within the region, yet the results depend on further actions.
Cross River Integrates Ripple’s RLUSD on the XRP Ledger
Cross River is implementing the USD-denominated RLUSD stablecoin from Ripple on the XRP Ledger within the bank’s core banking framework. This implementation is aimed at facilitating real-time settlement, cross-border payments, and 24/7 treasury transactions via one API.
This development connects to the larger topic of the Ripple BLOOM Initiative in the context of digital payments, although they are different initiatives. The BLOOM project is attempting to create common standards for cross-border payments. This initiative’s success will be dependent on regional cooperation, regulation, and adoption.

Quick Take
- Singapore’s BLOOM initiative has added the central banks of Malaysia and Thailand as policymaker members.
- Ripple, Visa, Mastercard, and the World Bank Group are also among the project’s participants, alongside Circle, Coinbase, and JPMorgan.
The central banks of Malaysia and Thailand are joining Singapore's BLOOM (Borderless, Liquid, Open, Online, Multi-currency) initiative to work on cross-border payments involving stablecoins and tokenized deposits.
Singapore's Monetary Authority (MAS) confirmed Friday that Bank Negara Malaysia and the Bank of Thailand had joined as policymaker members. Ripple, Visa, Mastercard, and the World Bank Group are also among the initiative's participants, alongside Circle, Coinbase, JPMorgan, Standard Chartered, and Stripe.
BLOOM began in October last year, with MAS bringing together banks and technology firms to test payments using tokenized bank money and regulated stablecoins. Singapore has separately tested a wholesale central bank digital currency.
Cross-border payments and settlement
Ripple first announced its participation in BLOOM in March, when it said it would test trade payments using RLUSD on the XRP Ledger. The trial with supply chain fintech firm Unloq uses its SC+ platform to automate payment releases when predefined conditions are met.
MAS said the work will focus on how banks handle different forms of digital money for cross-border transactions, how different networks can interoperate, and safeguards, including identity checks, sanctions screening, and transaction controls.
"The future of finance will involve multiple forms of digital money operating across different institutions and markets," MAS Deputy Managing Director Leong Sing Chiong said Friday.
Bank Negara Malaysia Deputy Governor Aznan bin Abdul Aziz said cross-border payments using multiple forms of digital money were becoming a more tangible prospect, while Bank of Thailand's Deputy Governor Daranee Saeju said BLOOM would help it examine regulatory approaches to tokenized money, particularly in cross-border payments and wholesale settlement.

BLOOM expands across borders
The Monetary Authority of Singapore said Bank Negara Malaysia and the Bank of Thailand joined Singapore's BLOOM cross-border digital money initiative as policymaker members on Friday. BLOOM, short for Borderless, Liquid, Open, Online, Multi-currency, was launched in October last year and the three central banks will work with industry players on common approaches for accepting, exchanging and settling digital money across institutions, networks and borders. BLOOM covers tokenised deposits, regulated stablecoins and settlement across payment networks, with a focus on interoperability and programmable controls.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore said shared frameworks would lower implementation costs and shorten time to market, while the authority said the three central banks would look at how international standards and jurisdiction-specific supervisory expectations can be applied to such transactions. The industry membership has expanded to include Airwallex, Mastercard, Maybank, Monee, Nium, Ripple, ShopeePay, Visa and the World Bank Group, alongside founding members such as DBS, OCBC and UOB.
What the central banks will do
The Monetary Authority of Singapore said the three central banks will center their work on three areas: acceptance and settlement across jurisdictions, interoperability between digital money arrangements, and programmable controls such as identity verification, sanctions screening and transaction controls. The Monetary Authority of Singapore said the initiative will examine how international standards and jurisdiction-specific supervisory expectations can be applied to transactions while leaving room for differences in local requirements. Bank Negara Malaysia separately outlined three pilot schemes, announced in February, to test a ringgit stablecoin and tokenised deposits for domestic and cross-border wholesale payments in 2026.
The Bank of Thailand's move aligns with a broader push among Southeast Asian monetary authorities to adopt distributed ledger technology, and the authority has not set a timeline for the common frameworks or said when the first cross-border transactions under the expanded membership would be processed. The Monetary Authority of Singapore said central bank involvement is meant to ensure public policy and regulatory considerations are built in as those approaches take shape.
Participants and potential impact
The Monetary Authority of Singapore said BLOOM's industry roster has grown beyond its founding group of Singapore lenders DBS, OCBC and UOB, along with Standard Chartered, JPMorgan Chase, Coinbase, StraitsX, Circle and Temasek. The Monetary Authority of Singapore said the initiative brings together policymakers, banks, payment networks and technology providers to push digital money into cross-border financial activity, and it said the World Bank Group's presence is expected to bring global experience in payment-system modernization, cross-border payments and financial inclusion. The Monetary Authority of Singapore said BLOOM builds on Project Orchid, a 2021 MAS effort to explore uses for a digital Singapore dollar, and the current phase focuses on the technical and policy plumbing needed for next-generation payments infrastructure.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore said the arrangement could eventually mean fewer bilateral integrations and a more uniform set of compliance expectations when moving tokenised value between markets. The Monetary Authority of Singapore said shared implementation frameworks and aligned commercial and operating arrangements would cut the need for financial institutions to strike separate deals with every counterparty or market, lowering implementation costs and shortening time to market.

With Malaysia and Thailand joining, the three central banks will work with industry participants to establish common approaches for accepting, exchanging and settling regulated stablecoins and tokenized bank deposits across borders.
Three Countries Target Easier Digital Payments
The partnership focuses on a major challenge for cross-border payments: different countries and financial institutions may use separate systems and rules to process digital money.
BLOOM will examine how transactions can be settled between institutions and markets, and how different digital money networks can work together. The initiative also aims to reduce the need for banks and payment firms to establish separate arrangements with every counterparty in each market.
This could lower implementation costs and help financial institutions introduce cross-border payment services faster. However, the announcement does not confirm an immediate launch of a shared stablecoin payment service.
Stablecoin Transfers to Include Safety Checks
The three central banks will also work with industry participants on safeguards such as identity verification, sanctions screening and transaction controls. The aim is to support cross-border digital money transfers while accounting for international standards and each country’s regulatory requirements.

SINGAPORE, Oct. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Building on its longstanding collaboration, Malaysian Investment Development Authority (MIDA), Singapore Business Federation (SBF) and CIMB Singapore yesterday concluded the inaugural Invest Malaysia Day 2026 in Singapore, bringing together over 200 businesses and investors in Singapore to explore investment insights, business advisory support and partnership opportunities across Malaysia. The forum underscored the growing importance of the Singapore-Malaysia economic relationship, connecting attendees with representatives from Malaysia's federal investment agencies, regional development authorities and ecosystem partners.
The forum was officiated by Guest-of-Honour Her Excellency Datin Paduka Anizan Siti Hajjar Adnin, High Commissioner of Malaysia to Singapore, who delivered the keynote address. Keynote addresses were also delivered by Malaysian state investment leaders YB Tuan Ng Sze Han of Selangor, YB Lee Ting Han of Johor and YB Dato' Mohamad Nizar bin Dato' Sri Mohamad Najib of Pahang. Mr. Lee Yee Fung of the Singapore Business Federation and Mr. Benjamin Tan of CIMB Singapore also addressed the participants.
"Malaysia offers Singapore businesses opportunities across diverse growth sectors, supported by well-established industrial ecosystems and strong regional connectivity. National initiatives such as the New Industrial Master Plan (NIMP) 2030, the National Energy Transition Roadmap (NETR) and the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) provide further avenues for investment across manufacturing, the digital economy, logistics, renewable energy, healthcare and advanced technologies.
As companies assess their next phase of growth, MIDA is committed to helping investors identify suitable locations, understand the regulatory and incentives landscape, and connect with the relevant federal and state agencies. Through this coordinated approach, we aim to facilitate investment decisions and support businesses in establishing and expanding their operations in Malaysia," said Datuk Sikh Shamsul Ibrahim Sikh Abdul Majid, Chief Executive Officer of MIDA.
The day's programme covered:
"Singapore and Malaysia share one of ASEAN's most interconnected economic partnerships, underpinned by deep trade, investment and business links. As Singapore prepares to assume the ASEAN Chairmanship next year, strengthening these connections will be key to unlocking new opportunities across the region," said Mr. Benjamin Tan, Head of Commercial and Transaction Banking, CIMB Singapore. "As part of a leading ASEAN bank group, CIMB Singapore is committed to supporting businesses in navigating cross-border opportunities and achieve their regional growth ambitions."

The strong engagement at Invest Malaysia Day 2026 reflects growing confidence in Malaysia's economic outlook and reinforces the importance of closer Singapore-Malaysia collaboration in driving regional growth and competitiveness.

Listed on Bursa Malaysia via CIMB Group Holdings Berhad, it had a market capitalisation of approximately RM80.1 billion as at 30 June 2026. It offers consumer banking, commercial banking, wholesale banking, transaction banking, Islamic banking and asset management products and services. articles.full_text:
On October 15, 2026, in Panama, the Vietnamese Trade Office in Mexico (also covering Panama) organized a Vietnam-Panama Trade Promotion Seminar. Attendees and speakers included Ms. Phan Thi Nga, representative of the Vietnamese Trade Office in Mexico (also covering Panama); Mr. Hardeep Singh Bhullar, Director of the Foreign Direct Investment Promotion Department, Ministry of Commerce and Industry of Panama (MICI); Ms. Regina Arauz Liakópulos, Honorary Consul of Vietnam in Panama; representatives from the Directorate General of Export Processing Zones/Foreign Trade Zones of Panama; the Director General of the Panamanian Investment Services Directorate; Mr. Servio Samudio, former Ambassador of Panama to Vietnam; and 30 representatives from Panamanian businesses and business associations.
Vietnam-Panama Trade Promotion Workshop: Expanding Opportunities for Trade, Investment, and Logistics Cooperation
The seminar, organized by the Vietnamese Trade Office in Mexico (also covering Panama), was held on October 15, 2026, in Panama City, with the participation of the Panamanian Ministry of Commerce and Industry (MICI). Its aim was to introduce Vietnam's economic and trade potential and connect businesses from both countries, following the official visit of the President of Panama to Vietnam.
In his opening remarks, the representative of the Vietnamese Trade Office in Mexico stated that the seminar was organized to introduce Vietnamese products to Panamanian businesses, helping them find suppliers and partners in Vietnam, and creating more trade and investment opportunities between the two countries. According to the representative of the Vietnamese Trade Office in Mexico, the seminar follows the official visit of Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino to Vietnam in early October 2026, the highest-level visit from Panama to Vietnam in 14 years. The visit yielded many important results: the two governments signed nine cooperation documents; identified priority areas including maritime, aviation, logistics - warehousing, insurance, agriculture , and trade; and agreed to initiate negotiations on an Investment Promotion and Protection Agreement. At the business forum in Hanoi, the President of Panama noted that Panama is entering the largest investment cycle of the century, with Vietnam producing goods and Panama connecting markets, facilitating the global flow of goods.
Regarding economic and trade relations, bilateral trade turnover increased from approximately US$5 million in 2005 to US$478 million in 2025. Of this, Vietnam exported approximately US$462 million to Panama and imported approximately US$15.5 million, indicating significant room for improvement in the trade balance. Ms. Nga also provided an overview of Vietnam's economy: GDP growth in the first nine months of 2026 is projected at approximately 9%; the population is around 103 million; and Vietnam currently has 17 free trade agreements with 60 economies. Although the two countries do not yet have a free trade agreement, Panama recognized Vietnam as a market economy in 2010, and they have agreements on visa exemption and double taxation avoidance.
The Vietnamese Trade Representative in Mexico emphasized the highly complementary nature of the two economies: Vietnam can serve as a bridge for Panama to access Asian markets, while Panama can help Vietnamese businesses connect with Latin American markets. Priority areas for cooperation include agriculture and fisheries (fruits, vegetables, seafood, rice), manufacturing, semiconductors, tourism, and investment. Currently, Panama has 14 investment projects in Vietnam. The Vietnamese Trade Representative in Mexico stated that the two governments have discussed the possibility of Vietnam reopening its embassy in Panama soon, and the Trade Representative hopes to do so at the same time. Panamanian businesses have also been invited to participate in the Vietnam International Sourcing program organized by the Vietnamese Ministry of Industry and Trade, scheduled for July 2027.
On the Panamanian side, Mr. Hardeep Singh Bhullar stated that Panama holds the position of "hub of hubs," boasting a network of over 23 free trade agreements and actively attracting foreign investment. He affirmed that the Panamanian Ministry of Commerce and Industry is ready to support investors and hopes that Vietnamese businesses will explore and invest in Panama. Ms. Regina Arauz Liakópulos, Honorary Consul of Vietnam in Panama, suggested that in addition to trade, strengthening cultural and people-to-people connections between the two countries is necessary; she also mentioned that the Panama Book Fair plans to invite Vietnam as a guest country.
At the seminar, representatives from the Panamanian Ministry of Commerce and Industry introduced two investment attraction policies. Firstly, the Free Trade Zone regime under Law 32/2011: Panama currently has 27 zones (20 operational, 7 under development) with over 200 businesses; businesses entering these zones do not require a minimum capital investment, licenses are free and unlimited, with a maximum license duration of 90 days; they are exempt from import duties on raw materials and machinery, income tax on exports, and ITBMS (VAT 7%); owners and shareholders are granted permanent residency from the outset. Secondly, there is the Qualified Investor Program: investors are granted permanent residency immediately upon approval, a process that takes approximately 60 days, with a minimum investment of $300,000 (first-time real estate sale), $500,000 (secondary real estate, state bank deposits, securities) or $750,000 (private bank deposits). According to the Panamanian Ministry of Commerce and Industry, the program has been operating for six years, attracting over 900 investors with a total capital exceeding $430 million.
During the discussion, delegates focused on post-licensing procedures, rules of origin, and traceability requirements for goods imported from Vietnam and re-exported to the US market. Representatives from the Panama Chamber of Commerce suggested that attracting Vietnamese investment should be linked to actual suppliers in Panama and industries with local raw materials, such as seafood processing. Panama affirmed its commitment to supporting investors and coordinating with the Vietnamese Trade Office to address any issues; the determination of the conversion rate required for goods to qualify as originating from Panama needs to be considered on a case-by-case basis.
Speaking at the seminar, Mr. Servio Samudio, former Ambassador of Panama to Vietnam, noted that Vietnam is a strong manufacturing country, while Panama is a connecting hub of the Americas, and the two economies complement each other. According to him, the relationship between the two countries is at a favorable point for promoting cooperation, and the long-term foundation of this relationship is the strong people-to-people connection.
The seminar was held immediately after the visit of the President of Panama to Vietnam, contributing to the concretization of commitments between the leaders of the two countries and opening up many opportunities for cooperation in trade, investment, and logistics between Vietnamese and Panamanian businesses.

articles.title: South China Sea Code of Conduct: A Deal Is Not Enough - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
articles.summary: South China Sea Code of Conduct: A Deal Is Not Enough  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

source_detail.name: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

articles.full_text:
As ASEAN and China work toward concluding a Code of Conduct (COC) for the South China Sea in 2026, the central question is not simply whether an agreement can be reached, but whether it will meaningfully reduce tensions. A deal is not enough if it does not address the underlying drivers of tension and shape actors’ behaviors.
The South China Sea is a contested maritime zone, involving China and ASEAN members Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Vietnam. To address the overlapping maritime claims and disputes, ASEAN and China have been negotiating a COC to establish a rules-based framework to manage maritime disputes, reduce miscalculations, and prevent armed conflict.
After nearly two decades of negotiations, Manila, as the current ASEAN chair, has recently signaled that agreement on the COC is at hand. A COC would represent an important diplomatic achievement.
Yet an agreement that lacks credible enforcement mechanisms, preserves ambiguity over compliance, or constrains Southeast Asian countries’ strategic autonomy could do little to address the region’s underlying security challenges.
The substance of the agreement matters more than announcing its completion. A COC that primarily reiterates commitments to dialogue, restraint, and peaceful dispute resolution – like those contained in the existing Declaration of Conduct – would have limited practical value. The COC needs clear procedures for managing incidents, resolving disagreements, and addressing violations.
The South China Sea has seen increased military activities. China has built a network of military facilities in the Spratly and Paracel Islands, some of which are now equipped to host bombers. In 2025, Vietnam commenced its own reclamation work on occupied features, building infrastructure to support a larger military presence.
Naval confrontations between China and the Philippines continue, highlighting the fragility of stability in the contested waters. Diplomatic commitments alone cannot guarantee responsible behavior
If the COC is to improve regional stability, it must include practical measures to prevent escalation and hold parties accountable for their conduct.
This raises a second challenge: ASEAN’s ability to ensure compliance. Even if the agreement includes specific obligations, its effectiveness will depend on whether parties are willing to implement them when doing so conflicts with their strategic interests. ASEAN’s consensus-based approach, while essential to maintaining regional unity, can complicate collective responses to violations, particularly when member states have different economic and security relationships with China.
A credible COC should therefore establish transparent procedures for reporting incidents, conducting consultations, and addressing alleged breaches. Regular reviews and clearly defined dispute-management channels could help prevent disagreements from escalating. Without a meaningful accountability mechanism, the COC risks just becoming a declaration of intent.
The agreement must also protect Southeast Asian states’ strategic autonomy. China may seek arrangements that limit activities it considers destabilizing, such as joint military exercises with the United States. Provisions governing military exercises, defense partnerships, or cooperation with external powers could create constraints that extend beyond managing disputes in the South China Sea. If drafted too broadly, the COC could inadvertently restrict ASEAN members’ ability to pursue their own security interests.
The challenge is to distinguish between measures designed to prevent maritime incidents and provisions that limit legitimate defense cooperation. Southeast Asian states should retain the freedom to conduct exercises, modernize their armed forces, and establish partnerships with countries outside the region, consistent with international law. A COC that undermines these freedoms would risk weakening the very strategic independence ASEAN seeks to preserve.
The Philippines’ expanding defense cooperation with non-Southeast Asian powers such as Australia and Japan illustrates this tension. Manila’s partnerships strengthen its deterrence capabilities and provide additional options for responding to maritime pressure. However, Beijing may view these arrangements as contributing to strategic competition, complicating efforts to reach a mutually acceptable agreement.
Nevertheless, external partnerships should not automatically be regarded as obstacles to a COC. They can strengthen Southeast Asian states’ negotiating position by showing that China and ASEAN alone cannot determine regional security, given the South China Sea’s significance as an international maritime trade route. Extra-regional powers’ participation in maritime security, however, should not obscure ASEAN’s central role in shaping regional norms.
Ultimately, the COC’s credibility will depend on whether it can reconcile three objectives: reducing tensions, ensuring compliance, and preserving the strategic autonomy of Southeast Asian countries. These objectives are not mutually exclusive, but achieving them will require precise language, practical implementation mechanisms, and a willingness to address violations consistently.
The measure of success, then, is not whether ASEAN and China can sign an agreement, but whether that agreement changes behavior at sea. Without credible commitments and meaningful accountability, the COC may secure a diplomatic milestone while failing to deliver the regional stability it promises.

SpaceX (SPCX) stock slid on Thursday, giving back Wednesday's post-earnings gain.
Shares jumped 7.8% on Wednesday following SpaceX's upbeat third quarter results and AI commentary.
The stock is under pressure — down 9% — along with the broader tech trade, following Meta (META) earnings and more headlines suggesting new strikes in the US/Israeli war with Iran.
As for SpaceX, it guided fourth quarter capital expenditures to $35 billion to $40 billion, up from $19.6 billion in the third quarter, as more compute capacity comes online. The company ended the quarter with $36.1 billion in debt.
"The earnings call served to amplify the enormous calls on capital that loom over the next few years," MoffettNathanson analyst Julie Zhu wrote in a note to clients.
"We are investment grade, have a very strong balance sheet, and there are a number of available pools of debt capital," SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said on the earnings call.
Then there's the merger talk. Musk said SpaceX and Tesla (TSLA) have each formed special committees of independent directors to study a tie-up, and that he is recused as a conflicted party. "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said.
That endorsement created a "mess" for the process, a person with direct knowledge of the talks told Reuters. Insiders worry the resulting shareholder scrutiny could delay talks by several weeks.
Bloomberg separately reported that the companies are aiming to announce a deal in the first half of 2027.
On the flip side, Wall Street is now more bullish on SpaceX's prospects. JPMorgan's Doug Anmuth more than doubled his price target to $500 from $240, citing AI infrastructure growth. BofA raised its target to $275 from $235.
Barclays analyst Dan Levy flagged Tesla's annual meeting, which must be held by Dec. 6, as the likely venue for a shareholder vote. He added that a deal announced in late October or early November could push approval out six to 12 months.

MANILA, Philippines —Infrastructure investment in the Philippines is expected to remain at around four percent of gross domestic product (GDP) through 2027 even as delayed public works projects resume, according to Japan Credit Rating Agency (JCR).
In its latest issuer report, the Japanese debt watcher projected infrastructure investment at 4.2 percent of GDP in 2026 and four percent in 2027. This would remain below the 4.7 percent or P1.32 trillion recorded in 2025 and the 5.8 percent seen in both 2023 and 2024.
Infrastructure investment covers spending on long-term public facilities and systems that support economic activity. Weak project implementation has weighed on construction, private investment and overall economic growth.
JCR attributed the slowdown to tighter scrutiny of Department of Public Works and Highways projects and payment procedures following irregularities in flood control projects.
The government has since strengthened project planning, budget allocation, procurement, construction verification and payments. JCR expects public infrastructure spending to recover in the second half as agencies use previously allocated budgets and reviewed projects resume.
“The economy is currently slowing due to a decline in the pace of public works projects and a drop in consumption caused by rising crude oil prices,” JCR said.
Economic growth slowed to 4.4 percent in 2025 and further eased to 2.6 percent in the first half of 2026 as public investment remained sluggish and elevated inflation weakened household spending. JCR expects full-year growth to settle in the mid-three-percent range before picking up over the medium term.
The report also provided further analysis supporting JCR’s decision on Aug. 28 to retain the Philippines’ A- investment-grade credit rating with a stable outlook. A sovereign credit rating reflects an agency’s assessment of a government’s capacity to repay its obligations.
JCR said progress in raising per capita income, upgrading industries, expanding domestic employment and sustaining infrastructure investment could support the rating. In contrast, any reversal in fiscal reforms would be a negative factor.
Meanwhile, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) welcomed JCR’s assessment that the country remained resilient to external shocks.
“JCR’s recognition of the country’s strong external buffers reflects confidence in the Philippine economy’s ability to weather global headwinds, including those arising from the Middle East conflict,” BSP Governor Eli Remolona Jr. said.
The country’s foreign exchange reserves, its stockpile of foreign currency assets and other reserve holdings, stood at $99.5 billion at end-September. The amount was enough to cover 6.2 months of imports and other external payments and was equivalent to 3.1 times the country’s short-term foreign debt falling due within a year.
“The BSP will continue to manage the country’s foreign exchange reserves prudently to help safeguard economic stability,” Remolona said.
JCR said the country’s external position was also supported by remittances and business process outsourcing revenues.
The debt watcher also noted that more than 60 percent of Philippine exports to the United States remained exempt from additional tariffs, while 23 free trade agreements in force or under negotiation helped diversify the country’s export markets.

articles.title: Vietnam's double-digit growth must not come at the cost of macroeconomic stability - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Vietnam's double-digit growth must not come at the cost of macroeconomic stability  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Vietnam’s GDP grew 9.01% in the first nine months of 2026, but the push for double-digit growth must not come at the expense of macroeconomic stability, with rising inflationary pressures and uneven growth among major economic hubs posing challenges to the 10% full-year target.
The 9.01% growth in nine months highlights the economy’s considerable momentum. However, the full-year target of 10% places significant pressure on the final quarter.
With much of the remaining growth requirement concentrated in the last few months, policymakers must not only stimulate production, investment and consumption, but also contain inflation and safeguard the economy’s key balances.
A report by state-controlled bank BIDV’s research team, led by economist Can Van Luc, forecasts GDP growth of 9.5-9.7% for 2026, with Q4 expansion of around 10.8-11.5%.
While positive, the forecast falls short of the pace needed to meet the 10% annual target, underscoring the challenges facing the economy in the final months of the year.
Inflation narrows policy room as major economic hubs lag
The push for faster growth comes as room to contain inflation is becoming more limited. Speaking at a National Assembly group discussion on Sunday on Vietnam’s economic performance in 2026 and plans for 2027, Prime Minister Le Minh Hung warned that rising inflation could erode the benefits of economic growth for households. He stressed that strong growth must be built on a foundation of stability.
The message is clear: growth cannot be pursued in isolation from macroeconomic stability. Its benefits must translate into jobs, incomes and purchasing power rather than be eroded by rising prices. Renewed inflationary pressure could also push up input and funding costs, weakening efforts to stimulate production, investment and consumption.
Economist Ngo Tri Long has also highlighted the limited room for maneuver in controlling inflation as price pressures intensify. With average consumer price inflation (CPI) rising 4.52% in the first nine months, policymakers must account for the risk that energy price volatility and higher input costs will feed through to consumer prices.
“Inflation control, therefore, requires coordination between fiscal and monetary policies, alongside measures to secure supply and reduce intermediary costs,” he stressed.
PM Hung also called for cuts in intermediary stages and input costs, faster administrative reforms, fewer business conditions and more efficient public investment disbursement. These measures could support near-term growth while strengthening the economy’s supply capacity. Unlocking resources, reducing business costs and improving investment efficiency would help generate growth without necessarily adding to inflationary pressure.
Growth, however, remains uneven across localities. According to the National Statistics Office, only 12 of Vietnam’s 34 provinces and cities recorded gross regional domestic product (GRDP) growth of at least 10% in the first nine months of 2026. Hanoi grew 8.85%, while Ho Chi Minh City expanded 9.06%, with both falling short of double-digit growth.
These figures highlight the importance of assessing growth not only by the number of localities recording high rates, but also by their economic size and contribution to national output.
A review report by the National Assembly’s Committee for Economic and Financial Affairs underscores the challenge posed by the country’s largest economic hubs. HCMC, Hanoi, Hai Phong and Dong Nai account for nearly 47% of national GRDP, yet all are projected to miss their 2026 growth targets. Given their substantial share of the economy, their underperformance places significant pressure on national growth, which faster expansion elsewhere may not fully offset.
At the legislature’s Sunday group discussion, HCMC Party Committee Secretary Tran Luu Quang said the national growth target would be difficult to achieve if the city fell short. If the city’s growth rate missed its target by one percentage point, the other 33 provinces and cities would each need to add around 0.25 percentage points to their growth rates to compensate, he said.
The calculation illustrates the city’s importance to the national growth outlook and the need for it to strengthen its role as a leading economic hub.
However, Quang also cautioned against pursuing growth at any cost, stressing the need to use resources efficiently and lay the groundwork for 2027 and beyond. The principle applies to economic management nationwide: the goal is not merely to accelerate growth in the short term, but also to preserve its quality and sustainability.
The challenge, therefore, is not simply to push every locality to grow faster, but to remove bottlenecks constraining major economic centers. Improving project execution, capital mobilization, market demand and businesses’ capacity to expand production will be crucial to strengthening their contribution to national growth. Other localities, meanwhile, need to build on their comparative advantages and improve growth quality rather than focus solely on headline targets.
Preserving macroeconomic stability for sustainable growth
BIDV’s forecast of 9.5-9.7% GDP growth puts Vietnam’s 2026 double-digit target to the test. The key is to identify the conditions needed to narrow the gap: resilient demand, investment that translates into productive capacity, stronger growth in major economic hubs and inflation that remains under control.
“We should make every effort, but 10% growth should not be pursued at any cost. GDP growth could reach 9.7-10% this year, providing an important foundation for high and sustainable growth in the years ahead,” Dr. Can Van Luc said.
His assessment places the emphasis on the quality of growth rather than the achievement of a single short-term target. Efforts to accelerate economic activity remain necessary, but must go hand in hand with efficient capital allocation, expanded productive capacity and resilience to external shocks.
Finance Minister Ngo Van Tuan reinforced this policy direction at the 33rd APEC Finance Ministers’ Meeting in Hong Kong on October 20-21, saying Vietnam would make macroeconomic stability the foundation for sustainable double-digit growth in 2027.
The minister cited several indicators for the first nine months of 2026, including GDP growth of 9.01%, CPI inflation of 4.52%, registered FDI of $50.36 billion, development investment spending accounting for around 40%, and public debt at 35-36% of GDP. Presented during fiscal policy discussions with international partners, the figures underscored the importance of maintaining macroeconomic stability and coordinating policies to support growth.
Targeted fiscal policy, working alongside flexible monetary policy, should focus on activities that generate added value, expand productive capacity and improve capital efficiency. Institutional reform, lower business costs, more effective public investment and a stronger private sector will also be critical to converting resources into sustainable economic gains.
The need to accelerate growth in Q4 remains pressing, but it cannot be separated from price stability and the efficient allocation of resources. Pursuing growth at any cost could increase inflation risks, raise funding costs and weaken investment quality, undermining the foundations for future expansion. By contrast, removing bottlenecks, improving the business environment and unlocking resources for production could help establish a more durable growth trajectory.
Vietnam’s 2026 growth drive is therefore not merely a final push towards a double-digit target, but also an opportunity to lay the groundwork for the next stage of development. Growth must be supported by macroeconomic stability, efficient resource use and resilience to external shocks. High growth remains an important objective, but it will be sustainable only if the economy can maintain momentum without undermining the conditions that that make that growth possible.

Rapid advances in science and technology, particularly artificial intelligence (AI), are fundamentally reshaping financial operations and governance, according to Assoc. Prof. Dr. Bui Huu Toan, Chairman of the Board of Trustees of the Banking Academy of Vietnam.
Delivering the opening address at the 11th Vietnam International Symposium in Banking and Finance (VSBF 2026) on October 22, Mr. Toan emphasized: "This dynamic presents a major practical challenge for Vietnam: how to accelerate growth while maintaining long-term sustainability, and how to aggressively integrate cutting-edge technologies while rigorously identifying, controlling, and mitigating risks. Rigorous academic research serves as the foundational knowledge base, providing vital empirical rationale to support macroeconomic governance by the State Bank of Vietnam and regulatory agencies."
The two-day VSBF 2026 symposium was jointly organized by the Banking Academy of Vietnam, the International Society for the Advancement of Financial Economics (ISAFE), and the Association of Vietnamese Scientists and Experts (AVSE Global). The event convened leading domestic and international regulatory experts, economists, and researchers for in-depth academic deliberations.
In addition to breakout plenary and technical sessions, the symposium featured a dedicated "Meet the Editors" panel, which addressed emerging operational themes such as integrating AI tools into academic research and navigating global academic publishing standards.
Offering an international perspective, Prof. Dr. Sabri Boubaker, representative of the Journal of International Financial Management & Accounting, noted that VSBF transcends the conventional presentation of research papers. Its core mission is fostering an environment that stimulates intellectual exchange, expands global research networks, and links Vietnamese scholars domestically and abroad with high-level international academia.
Prof. Boubaker underscored that the global financial landscape is undergoing deep structural shifts. The proliferation of AI, rapid technological breakthroughs, and intensifying mandates for sustainable transitions are presenting markets with unprecedented scenarios. Consequently, maintaining multifaceted dialogue platforms like VSBF that bridge academic theory with regulatory practice has become necessary.
Echoing this sentiment, Prof. Dr. Nguyen Duc Khuong, Chairman of AVSE Global, highlighted the remarkable resilience and recovery capacity of the Vietnamese economy. Despite global geopolitical headwinds, Vietnam continues to maintain its standing among the region's most dynamic and fast-expanding economies. Notably, national import-export turnover in the first nine months reached approximately $888 billion, underscoring high trade openness running at nearly double projected GDP.
Furthermore, aggressive investments in strategic national infrastructure—including seaports, international airports, and inter-regional logistics corridors—alongside streamlined administrative apparatus reforms are establishing a solid foundation for Vietnam's upcoming development phase.
Active compliance with environmental, social, and governance (ESG) standards alongside the operational launch of Vietnam's International Financial Center provide prime conduits to capture high-quality green FDI inflows, advancing Vietnam's commitment to net-zero emissions by 2050 and its strategic objective of attaining high-income developed nation status by 2045.

| The Saigon Beer production line at one of SABECO’s breweries. — Photos courtesy of SABECO | 
HÀ NỘI — As Việt Nam pursues ambitious growth targets while ensuring long-term sustainability, the role of large businesses is increasingly being measured not only by their financial performance and tax contributions, but also by their ability to create jobs, strengthen domestic supply chains and improve the economy’s competitiveness.
With an established business foundation and an extensive nationwide network, Saigon Beer – Alcohol – Beverage Corporation (SABECO) illustrates how a major enterprise can generate economic value across multiple areas.
Large enterprises play an important role in generating State budget revenue, leading industry value chains and creating business opportunities for their partners.
At the 10th announcement ceremony for products recognised under the Vietnam National Brand Programme in 2026, Prime Minister Lê Minh Hưng emphasised the need to shift from individual development towards greater collaboration and joint efforts to upgrade Vietnamese value chains.
“Large enterprises should lead their ecosystems and support small- and medium-sized enterprises in improving technology, quality and management capacity," the PM said.
"Through healthy cooperation and resource sharing, businesses can build stronger industries and supply chains.”
SABECO is among the businesses contributing to this goal, combining its financial contributions with efforts to support the wider network of suppliers, distributors and other partners connected to its operations.
Economic contributions extend beyond tax payments
According to the recently released VNTAX200 ranking, SABECO ranked 14th among Việt Nam’s 200 largest taxpayers in 2025, with actual tax payments of more than VNĐ14.9 trillion (US$577 million).
The ranking reflects the company’s ability to sustain its operations amid challenges facing the beverage industry and the broader business environment.
SABECO reported net revenue of nearly VNĐ25.9 trillion in 2025, alongside pre-tax profit of VNĐ5.65 trillion and after-tax profit of VNĐ4.57 trillion. Its return on equity (ROE) stood at 19.3 per cent.
While tax payments provide a direct measure of a company’s contribution to public finances, the broader economic impact of major businesses such as SABECO also lies in the value chains and business networks they support nationwide.
In 2025, 94 per cent of SABECO’s total procurement spending went to domestic partners and suppliers. More than 85 per cent of its core raw-material suppliers were Vietnamese businesses.
Prioritising domestic suppliers helps circulate business revenue through local production networks, supporting sectors including manufacturing, packaging, transportation and logistics.
The company also provides jobs for more than 7,700 people through its breweries and nationwide distribution network. Its extensive value chain generates business opportunities for a range of partners, from raw-material suppliers and transport operators to distributors and retailers.
Investing in long-term competitiveness
To sustain their economic contributions over time, manufacturing businesses must look beyond their existing scale. Adapting to market changes, improving productivity and expanding business opportunities are essential to maintaining competitiveness.
At SABECO, this approach is reflected in increased investment in research and development (R&D), production technology, operational efficiency and export expansion.
| SABECO deploys supply chain management systems to strengthen operational oversight. | 
The company is accelerating digital transformation across its value chain, deploying warehouse management systems (WMS), transportation management systems (TMS) and commercial data platforms to improve operational monitoring, control costs and support decision-making.
Alongside consolidating its domestic market position, SABECO is expanding its export business. In the first half of 2026, export turnover reached 139 per cent of its target for the period, marking a 221.2 per cent increase year-on-year.
The company aims to increase the contribution of export markets to double-digit levels over the next five years.
As Việt Nam pursues its next phase of economic growth, businesses capable of generating value across multiple areas are expected to play an increasingly important role.
Beyond contributing to State budget revenue, they can help strengthen domestic production, create jobs, support supply chain partners and improve the economy’s overall competitiveness.

articles.full_text:
The South Korean electronics giant is considering expanding India production, including making fresh investments, to boost exports from here. But if the international market continues to contract due to the high cost of memory chips, it could explore a shift of capacity.
Also Read: Price shock trumps festive cheer as India smartphone shipments hit decade low
Numbers Reflect Strategy
Samsung may shift production from countries like Vietnam to take advantage of the incentive scheme, the people told ET.
Also Read: Apple India in sweet spot as FY26 revenue crosses Rs 1 lakh crore, profit soars
Unlike Apple, which exports more than 70% of its India production, Samsung has been shipping only around 40-50% to markets abroad.
As per industry data, it exported about $21.2 billion worth of phones from India since FY2020-21, when the country implemented a production-linked incentive (PLI) scheme for mobile phones. While the highest exports were $4.4 billion in FY24-25, exports dropped to around $4 billion in FY25-26, when the company was not part of the PLI scheme, having completed its five-year tenure in FY24-25.
The company started increasing exports again this fiscal year, even as the government announced the new five-year Rs 62,300 crore scheme.
To become eligible for incentives under the new scheme, an existing brand must increase annual sales by a minimum of Rs 5,000 crore in each year of the scheme period, with the base being fiscal 2026.
For instance, to become eligible for the incentives in FY27, Samsung's sales must increase by Rs 5,000 crore from total sales in FY26. For FY28, the increase should be at least Rs 10,000 crore from the base year, and for the final year in FY31, it should be Rs 25,000 crore.
While the scheme does not specifically promote exports, it has been framed in a way that exporting more will draw higher incentives. The scheme offers incentives in the range of 2.5% to 5%, with an additional 1.5% to companies that use locally manufactured components like display and camera modules, enclosures, batteries and USB cables.
An industry executive said the company would be utilising its capacity spread across factories globally for making phones, including the hub in Vietnam, depending on cost efficiencies. With stress in the mobile phone market due to memory price shocks, production would, however, be aligned to a country that offers the best value, he said.
Vietnam Global Hub
Samsung has one of its largest factories in Noida, but Vietnam remains the global hub for manufacturing and exports. Unlike Apple, which has been gradually shifting iPhone production from China to India, Samsung is not shifting production from Vietnam where it has a well-developed ecosystem. The company, however, is also expanding in India organically and is already a participant in the component manufacturing scheme.
Application window for the new scheme opened on October 15 and companies are expected to apply in the coming months if they want to claim incentives for the current fiscal year. The application window will remain open till March 31, 2029.
The government expects the new scheme to help increase domestic value addition in smartphones to 40-45% by the end of the scheme from 24% now.
It projects cumulative mobile-phone production of Rs 39 lakh crore and exports of Rs 15 lakh crore during its scheme period, creating an estimated 600,000 new direct jobs.
The previous PLI scheme helped production reach Rs 22 lakh crore and exports over Rs 7.5 lakh crore. It is estimated to have created 1.2 million jobs.
Under the previous scheme, the government disbursed Rs 19,090 crore in incentives, and collected Rs 25,000 crore in direct tax and Rs 3 lakh crore in GST from the smartphone industry.

articles.title: Manufacturing Shift from China to India: Key Reasons - Business Outreach Magazine
articles.summary: Manufacturing Shift from China to India: Key Reasons  Business Outreach Magazine
articles.full_text:
For three decades, “made in China” was simply how the world’s electronics, cars and clothes got made. That machine hasn’t broken down. But a growing number of multinational companies no longer want to depend on it alone.
The manufacturing shift from China to India has picked up real pace over the last two years. Tariff shocks, pandemic-era shutdowns and unease about relying on one country for critical production pushed boardrooms to ask a hard question: what if China becomes harder to work with tomorrow? India, with its scale, its incentives and a fast-growing consumer base, has become one of the loudest answers.
This piece looks at why the manufacturing shift from China to India is happening now, and where India still has work to do before it can call itself a genuine alternative.
Quick Glance
| Factor | Why It Matters | 
| China Plus One Strategy | Spreads production across more than one country | 
| PLI scheme and Make in India | Rewards investment tied to real output | 
| Electronics Manufacturing in India | Fastest-growing proof point of the shift | 
| Global Supply Chain Diversification | Cuts exposure to any single country’s problems | 
| Foreign Direct Investment in India | Signals long-term confidence, not just a trend | 
China Plus One Isn’t a Buzzword Anymore
The China Plus One Strategy sounds like consultant-speak, but the logic is simple: keep China operations running, and build a second production base elsewhere so one bad year doesn’t sink the whole supply chain.
Container ships stuck outside ports, factories shut for weeks during COVID-19, components that couldn’t be sourced for months, tariff back-and-forth between the US and China all of it made the case too strong to ignore. Here’s what’s actually pushing the shift:
- Cutting reliance on a single country for critical production
- Managing tariff and geopolitical risk
- Building a backup line that can absorb shocks
- Getting closer to new, fast-growing consumer markets
India isn’t the only beneficiary; Vietnam, Mexico and Indonesia compete for the same investment. But India’s scale gives it an edge smaller economies can’t match, which is why the China Plus One Strategy so often ends with a factory in Gujarat, Tamil Nadu or Uttar Pradesh. It rarely means leaving China entirely; companies are simply refusing to put every egg in one basket.
Government Policy Is Doing the Heavy Lifting
India Manufacturing Growth over the last five years hasn’t happened by accident; deliberate policy has shaped it as much as market forces have.
The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme sits at the centre, with a total outlay of roughly ₹1.91 lakh crore across 14 sectors, tying cash incentives directly to what a company produces and exports. According to the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, as of March 31, 2026, the scheme had drawn actual investments of more than ₹2.40 lakh crore, generated over 14.15 lakh direct and indirect jobs, and pushed exports past ₹15.2 lakh crore since inception. That’s the kind of number that makes Foreign Direct Investment in India look like a working strategy rather than a policy slogan, spanning mobile phones, pharmaceuticals, automobiles and telecom equipment.
The government’s Make in India push has run alongside the PLI scheme since 2014, nudging sectors toward higher local value addition. Neither works alone a company still weighs the incentive against land costs, power, logistics and clearance timelines.
Electronics Manufacturing in India Is Where the Shift Shows Up Most
If one industry proves the manufacturing shift from China to India is real, it’s electronics.
Apple began assembling iPhones in India in 2017, before the PLI scheme even existed, but the scheme accelerated everything after. Apple now runs five iPhone assembly plants in India three under Tata Group entities, two under Foxconn – backed by a supplier network of close to 45 companies, according to Angel One’s February 2026 reporting. India assembled iPhones worth roughly $22 billion in the year to March 2025, up nearly 60% year-on-year, with $17.4 billion exported, per IBEF. By calendar 2025, iPhone exports had climbed to $23 billion, making the iPhone India’s single most valuable export product that year, per Business Today’s April 2026 coverage.
Tariffs pushed this along. Techwire Asia reported in March 2026 that China-assembled iPhones faced US import duties near 55%, against roughly 10% for India-made devices a gap wide enough that Apple reportedly chartered cargo flights in March 2025 to move close to $2 billion worth of India-made iPhones to the US ahead of fresh tariffs.
Competition inside Apple’s own supply chain shows how fast Electronics Manufacturing in India has matured. Tata Electronics, a late entrant that only started assembling iPhones after acquiring Wistron’s India unit in November 2023, has nearly caught up to Foxconn on exports over the five-year PLI period through FY26:
| Metric (FY22–FY26, PLI period) | Figure | 
| Tata Electronics: exported iPhone value | $26.3 billion | 
| Foxconn: exported iPhone value | $25.6 billion | 
| Foxconn: domestic-market iPhone value | $12.4 billion | 
| Tata Electronics: domestic-market iPhone value | $6.3 billion | 
| Apple India vendor component exports to China (FY26) | ~$2.5 billion, rising toward $3.5 billion | 
Source: Business Standard, July 2026; The Week, May 2026. A reversal is underway on that last line India’s component makers are now shipping parts to China rather than the other way round, something that would have sounded far-fetched only a few years ago. China still assembles most of the world’s iPhones, but the direction here is unmistakable.
Diversification, Workforce and Home Demand
Global Supply Chain Diversification answers what the pandemic exposed a single-location supply chain breaks the moment one link fails. A company running plants in both China and India can shift output if a strike, lockdown or tariff hits one location.
India’s other advantages reinforce that logic:
- A large, young workforce and a growing pool of engineers though productivity and technical skill matter more than headcount
- A domestic market for smartphones, cars and appliances large enough to justify local production on its own
- Local manufacturing that feeds Foreign Direct Investment in India by letting companies serve consumers at home while building export capacity in parallel
Automotive and Semiconductors: The Next Frontier
India’s established automotive sector gives it a real shot at fresh investment in EV components, batteries and power electronics.
Semiconductors are the longer game. India is building that ecosystem largely from scratch Tata Electronics alone has committed roughly ₹1.26 trillion toward semiconductor fabrication and ATMP facilities, per Business Standard’s July 2026 reporting. Nobody expects India to rival Taiwan soon, but the investment suggests India Manufacturing Growth is climbing the value chain, not just assembling.
What India Still Has to Fix
The opportunity is real, but so are the gaps:
- Infrastructure – power, roads, ports has improved unevenly across states
- The supplier ecosystem is still thin next to China’s dense clusters of component makers
- Several industries still import raw materials they could eventually make at home
- Vocational training hasn’t kept pace with the ambition behind Make in India
- Regulatory friction – land acquisition, environmental clearances, state-level tax rules still slows decisions on billion-dollar factories, where predictability often matters more than the incentive itself
Is India Actually Replacing China?
Not really, and framing it that way misses the point. China still has a mature supplier network, decades of know-how, and industrial clusters that took generations to build none of that disappears because a few factories move to Gujarat. What’s changing is India’s share of the pie, not China’s position at the top. Some multinationals will keep manufacturing in China while adding India capacity; others will make India their base for specific products, the way Apple has with iPhones bound for the US. The likely outcome, years out, is multiple manufacturing hubs rather than one country doing everything.
Key Takeaways
- The manufacturing shift from China to India runs on the China Plus One Strategy, not a wholesale exit from China.
- The PLI scheme and Make in India have turned Foreign Direct Investment in India into measurable output.
- Electronics Manufacturing in India, led by Apple’s supply chain, is the clearest proof point.
- Global Supply Chain Diversification is a multi-year process, not an overnight switch.
- India still has real gaps in infrastructure, supplier depth, skills and regulation.
Conclusion
The manufacturing shift from China to India isn’t one event it’s the sum of smaller decisions: a tariff calculation here, a PLI application there, a supplier relationship built over two years. Supply chain diversification, government incentives, a large workforce and a genuinely large domestic market have pushed in the same direction at roughly the same time, and that convergence is what makes the shift feel real.
Apple’s expanding iPhone production is the clearest evidence, but automotive components, pharmaceuticals and semiconductors are moving along a similar path, just earlier on. If India keeps attracting investment while closing its supplier, skills and infrastructure gaps, India Manufacturing Growth could become one of the more consequential economic stories of this decade not because India replaced China, but because the world stopped betting everything on one country.

Tariff risk, geopolitical uncertainty, pandemic-era disruptions, incentives like the PLI scheme, and India’s large consumer market are the main drivers.

"Under the unique 'one country, two systems' principle, Hong Kong enjoys both the China advantage and the global advantage. We are the only common law jurisdiction in China, our country, and have a legal and regulatory regime similar to most of the world's top financial hubs."

He said that Hong Kong would leverage its unique advantages under the "one country, two systems" principle, and make full use of its diverse financing channels and professional services as an international financial centre to serve as a "super connector" and "super value-adder". 
"Regionally, we need open channels for trade and investment, not new barriers. Connected markets allow capital to reach productive uses and technologies be adopted across borders," Mr Chan said during a plenary session on Global and Regional Economic and Financial Outlook (October 20).

The itineraries included visits to the Peak, Hong Kong Museum of Art, Hong Kong Palace Museum, Xiqu Centre, Chinese Culinary Institute and Ocean Park as well as a boat tour to enjoy the renowned views of Victoria Harbour.

A visit by a Tuoi Tre (Youth) online newspaper reporter to the UNESCO-listed heritage town on Thursday morning revealed a subdued tourism scene, with far fewer visitors than in previous years.
At 9:30 am, such streets as Tran Phu, Nguyen Thai Hoc and Bach Dang, which are typically crowded with tourists, were relatively deserted.
A few small tour groups followed their guides through the historic quarter, while most other visitors explored independently.
Even iconic attractions such as Cau Pagoda and Nguyen Thi Minh Khai Street appeared unusually quiet.
Pham Thi Ngoc, an employee at a shop on Tran Phu Street, said Hoi An normally enters its low tourism season from September onward.
However, she noted that the decline in visitors this year has been significantly more pronounced than in previous years.
“There are times when not a single tourist can be seen along an entire street, with only street vendors and sanitation workers around,” Ngoc said.
“This situation has persisted for about a month.”
Images of deserted streets have circulated widely on social media, attracting considerable attention.
“Where are all the tourists? Why is Hoi An so empty? I just don’t understand,” one local vendor wrote on Facebook alongside a photograph of a quiet street.
Accommodation providers and workshop operators in Hoi An have also confirmed that the unusually low number of visitors is a real concern this year.
Le Quoc Viet, vice-chairman of the Da Nang Tourism Association, attributed the downturn partly to economic difficulties.
He also pointed to the impact of media coverage of flooding and extreme weather during Hoi An’s 2025 flood season, which may have heightened travellers’ concerns about visiting the town.
Tran Thi Tuyet Dinh, owner of a local lodging facility, said cancellations for October and November this year were some 50 percent higher than in the same period last year.
Fear of flooding and natural disasters has made tourists more hesitant to visit the ancient town during this time of year, she explained.
“Our hotel is doing its best to provide guests with the highest standard of care,” she said.
“The weather has been beautiful this year, with plenty of sunshine, making it ideal for sightseeing. Yet there are so few visitors.”
The ancient town recorded over 121,400 paid sightseeing visits between September 6 and October 10, according to the Hoi An World Cultural Heritage Conservation Center.
Of these, 110,690 were international visitors.
Ticket sales generated more than VND14.1 billion (US$545,740).
In an effort to attract more visitors, the center is preparing to launch two themed tours, including ‘Exploring Hoi An’s Architectural Heritage’ and ‘Imprints of Traditional Tuong (classical Vietnamese opera).’
The programs are intended to enrich the cultural experiences available to tourists.
The center is also working with relevant authorities to step up inspections and address problems involving street vendors, persistent solicitation and aggressive attempts to attract customers.
In addition, it is reviewing and reorganising several boat-ticket sales points along the Hoai River to make sightseeing more convenient.
According to an April report by digital travel platform Agoda, Hoi An ranked first among slow-travel destinations in Asia.
As more international tourists seek meaningful connections rather than packed itineraries, the historic town on the Thu Bon River in Da Nang City has emerged as an ideal destination for a more relaxed style of travel.
Hoi An's appeal lies in a combination of qualities that few destinations can easily replicate.
Its ancient quarter is compact enough to explore on foot or by bicycle, yet rich enough in history, culture and scenery to keep visitors engaged for weeks.
Lantern-lit streets, the tranquil Thu Bon River, and lush green rice fields create a distinctive natural environment that offers a welcome escape from the pace of urban life.
The town also reflects Vietnam's long history of international trade through its diverse architecture, shaped by Vietnamese, Chinese, Japanese and Western influences.
Its varied cuisine, meanwhile, draws on the many cultures that have contributed to its development.
This cultural fusion gives Hoi An an identity of its own, making it more than simply a sightseeing destination.
It is a place where travellers can slow down, immerse themselves in local life and develop a deeper connection with the destination.
